kind: adversarial review of my own findings, before the close was drafted -- each load-bearing claim re-tested by a mechanism other than the one that produced it

attackOnMyOwnLoadBearingFindings.finding: T2 -- P-201 does not refuse an instantiated, unfilled county; it labels all 65 rails excluded-*.
attackOnMyOwnLoadBearingFindings.methodThatProducedIt: Executed the extracted production modules (_) against a synthetic full-shaped all-unaccounted fixture.
attackOnMyOwnLoadBearingFindings.secondAttack: Cross-checked by reading who calls what instead of running anything: git grep for assertPublishableCounty and evaluatePopulation( across factory src returned the export line and the definition, no call site. Then read bastrop-publish.mjs's imports and found requirePreBakeReadiness as the real publish refusal, and read evaluatePreBakeReadiness's own body, which tests only row.verdict === 'refuse' -- so every P-201 value clears. Two independent mechanisms, same conclusion.
attackOnMyOwnLoadBearingFindings.weakestLink: The synthetic fixture is mine, not a store read. If a real instantiated county also carries cells of another kind (e.g. one absent-verified cell per rail), the verdicts could differ. I could not test the real case because no store DSN is mounted. Stated as a condition on the finding, not hidden: the claim proven is 'an all-unaccounted instantiated county passes', which is exactly what the scope asserts and exactly what its own violation test specifies.

attackOnMyOwnLoadBearingFindings.finding: T3 -- the scope's 'depthWarmPromoted' instruction names a field no surface reads (it is depthWarmPromotion, a string marker).
attackOnMyOwnLoadBearingFindings.methodThatProducedIt: git grep across four repos for depthWarmPromoted / depthWarmPromotion / isDepthWarmPromoted, then git show of each hit's own lines.
attackOnMyOwnLoadBearingFindings.secondAttack: Read the L-B instrument's own SQL and its own in-memory shape side by side and found the two names in the SAME file (SQL: body->>'depthWarmPromotion'; classifier: envelope.depthWarmPromoted). That is a stronger form of the finding than the cross-repo version: the mismatch exists inside one artifact, so it is not an artefact of my grep being incomplete.
attackOnMyOwnLoadBearingFindings.weakestLink: I did not read every consumer of the envelope atom body; a fourth consumer could use a third spelling. That strengthens rather than weakens the finding (it is the divergence count, not the mismatch, that is uncertain). Reported as 'four predicates, no divergence test between any pair' with the four named.

attackOnMyOwnLoadBearingFindings.finding: T3 -- A-157 refutes the P-216 attribution the scope still teaches.
attackOnMyOwnLoadBearingFindings.secondAttack: Read the code the incident was about (hauska-map atom-chain-to-facets.ts's three-branch envelope decision, and LDT's reconcileAtomEnvelope.ts) and found the code supports the falsifier, not the correction: the envelope-unverified branch carries no geojson and sets envelopeCovered = false, so it does not 'keep the envelope drawn'. Also found the register already carries the corrected diagnosis as a candidate class ('stale client state after a server rollback masquerading as a server regression'). Three sources: the correction file, the code, the register.
attackOnMyOwnLoadBearingFindings.weakestLink: The branch is reached only when !envelope, so whether the map is a suppression mechanism depends on what envelope is bound to -- which I could not determine without reading further into the function's caller. Reported as an explicit open binding with the file and the branch named, rather than resolved in either direction. This is the one place in the review where I deliberately decline to give a verdict and say why.

attackOnMyOwnLoadBearingFindings.finding: T5 -- there is no cost telemetry anywhere in the factory.
attackOnMyOwnLoadBearingFindings.methodThatProducedIt: git grep -in for cost/dollars/cpu/gb-seconds across factory src, plus reading publish_runs' CREATE TABLE.
attackOnMyOwnLoadBearingFindings.secondAttack: Every hit from the grep was a PROPERTY dollar value, which is itself the trap (a naive grep for 'dollars' returns 30 hits and all of them are marketValue). I read the hits rather than counting them, then confirmed from the schema, then confirmed from two independent documents (A-179's 'no row or cost telemetry' for the two depth writers; the register's candidate class 'a completed write leaves no durable execution record once its lease is released'). Four mechanisms.
attackOnMyOwnLoadBearingFindings.weakestLink: Absence of a column is provable by reading the migrations and grep; absence of a COST SOURCE anywhere (e.g. a Cloud Run billing export read by some job) is not, because I did not read every job. The claim as written -- 'no cost telemetry in the factory store or its writers' -- is what I proved; 'no cost is measurable anywhere in the portfolio' is not claimed.

attackOnMyOwnLoadBearingFindings.finding: T6 -- C7 (46 instances) and C14 (16 instances) have no executable check; 18 of 19 class labels have zero executable checks today.
attackOnMyOwnLoadBearingFindings.methodThatProducedIt: Read the smooth path in full and mapped every class to its named check and stage.
attackOnMyOwnLoadBearingFindings.secondAttack: Computed the union class counts from both register halves as data and sorted them, so the largest classes (C9 133, C7 46, C4 38, C18 31, C8 26, C11 25) are ranked by their own numbers rather than by narrative prominence -- C7 being the third-largest AND unowned is the finding, and it is only visible this way. Also verified the register's arithmetic reconciles exactly (361 = 330 + 31; 125 = 125; union 486), so the counts I am ranking on are sound.
attackOnMyOwnLoadBearingFindings.weakestLink: The claim 'no executable check' is a claim about the smooth path's text and about the named files' existence. I verified the text; I verified that scripts/registry-divergence.mjs and scripts/ruling-implementation-check.mjs are not present in doc_repo. A check existing under a different name or in a product repo would refute it, and I did not grep every product repo for every proposed control. Stated as a condition.

attackOnMyOwnLoadBearingFindings.finding: T7 -- R5 depends on R1, which the same table defers to after Phase 2.
attackOnMyOwnLoadBearingFindings.methodThatProducedIt: Read section 4.2's ordered list and its R-table's Depends column.
attackOnMyOwnLoadBearingFindings.secondAttack: Topologically sorted the whole of sections 4.1-4.6 by hand from the Depends columns alone, without reading what the rows do, and the two R1 cycles plus the S6 three-way convergence fell out of the graph. That is a structural read of the plan, independent of the narrative.
attackOnMyOwnLoadBearingFindings.weakestLink: 'Deferred' could be read as 'not blocking the row's Depends' if the deferral is read as applying only to Phase 0 dispatch order rather than to the dependency. I report it as a textual contradiction inside section 4.2 and quote both sentences, so a reader can judge; I do not claim to know the author's intent.

attackOnMyOwnLoadBearingFindings.finding: T4 -- two surfaces keep a legacy value or fabricate a basis when a cell is unaccounted.
attackOnMyOwnLoadBearingFindings.methodThatProducedIt: git grep for 'unaccounted' across LDT serve files, then git show of the two files.
attackOnMyOwnLoadBearingFindings.secondAttack: The strongest possible corroboration was already in the corpus in the form of two TEST NAMES, which is independent of the source comments: cadRollFactFromParcelRecord.test.ts:111 ('a refused cell (unaccounted) returns null -- caller keeps the legacy value') and agValuationFactFromParcelRecord.test.ts:160 ('unaccounted ... refuses, never a fabricated absence or present'). The tests are the second mechanism; the source comments are the first; they agree on the two safe rails and the two unsafe ones.
attackOnMyOwnLoadBearingFindings.weakestLink: I inferred the customer-visible consequence (the legacy value reaching a customer) from the caller-keeps-legacy contract without reading the caller. Marked as inference in the review, with the file:line that would settle it.

attackOnMyOwnLoadBearingFindings.finding: T8 -- 9 of 15 L-E defects and 7 of 11 X-items have no owning row.
attackOnMyOwnLoadBearingFindings.methodThatProducedIt: Mapped section 4.5/4.5b items to rows named in the scope and OPS-16.
attackOnMyOwnLoadBearingFindings.secondAttack: Counted the row ids appearing inside section 4.5b by grep (P-248 for X1, P-250 for X3, and no others) rather than trusting my own mapping -- the conclusion is in the text, not in my reading of it.
attackOnMyOwnLoadBearingFindings.weakestLink: An item with a repo and no row could still be 'owned' in the sense that the item exists in the scope. I take the mission's bar ('list every defect no row owns') literally: an item that cannot be carded, dispatched, closed or probe-gated is not a row. Stated explicitly so the overseer can disagree with the bar rather than with the counting.

attackOnMyOwnLoadBearingFindings.finding: T9 item 5 -- the FAN-DEPTH commit gate does not fire in a Cursor session.
attackOnMyOwnLoadBearingFindings.methodThatProducedIt: Read .claude/settings.json's hook registration and A-181's own named-bypass list.
attackOnMyOwnLoadBearingFindings.secondAttack: Checked the filesystem-level alternative the gate would need and found none: no .git/hooks/pre-commit in this worktree, and git config core.hooksPath empty. A PreToolUse/Bash matcher is a tool-use hook, not a git hook; without either a git hook or the harness loading .claude/hooks, a `git commit` from a plain shell is unmediated. This is a self-implicating finding -- it means my own subAgents declaration would not have been caught had it been false.
attackOnMyOwnLoadBearingFindings.weakestLink: Whether Cursor loads .claude/settings.json hooks is asserted by A-181's own bypass text ('Cursor and any harness that does not load .claude/hooks') and NOT independently tested by me -- testing it would require attempting a violating commit, which the mission forbids. The filesystem evidence (no git hook) is mine; the Cursor claim is A-181's and is attributed.

Reason: FACTORY_DATABASE_URL_RO and ATOMS_DATABASE_URL are unset in this session. The review names the query each depends on and marks each UNMEASURED BY THIS LANE.

L-D's capacity facts beyond what A-179 restates (the frozen target pair, publish_runs/leases partitioning): I verified the target-pair freeze only as far as A-179 states it, and did NOT read publish-target-env.mjs or writer-target-env.mjs myself. The review does not rest a verdict on the frozen pair.
The 2026-08-28 read-timeout incident itself: cited from the dispatch and A-179/scope section 13, not re-read from a primary incident record.
The 24 commits and ~93 artifacts on seat/dispatch-planner (A-176): listed as a missing-item precondition in T10 where relevant, otherwise untouched.
Whether my 7-city public-source sample generalises to the 54. It does not, and the review says so twice (n=7, extrapolation flagged, Hallsburg's classification marked low-confidence).
Whether the quarantined branches are still disabled today: read from the two quarantine records' own 'after' blocks, not live-read against the Neon API.

verdictTally.note: No thesis held unconditionally. T5 is split: 'safe' holds with conditions, 'measurable' does not survive.

mostImportantThingInThisReview: That the plan's law names the wrong gate. The program preamble attaches 'proven by violation on an instantiated, unfilled county' to P-201, and P-201 is real and landed work that does the narrower thing its own row carded. But the function the preamble names, evaluatePublishGate, has no production caller at all, and the gate that actually refuses a publish would clear a county whose every rail reads excluded-not-applicable. A row was allocated, executed, merged and reported closed against a sentence in the law that the row could not have satisfied. Restating law 2 correctly costs one paragraph and prevents the next county's verdict from being trusted on the wrong mechanism.
